title: Nonmonotonic control of pattern formation by chemotaxis
abstract: We investigate pattern formation in generic two-species reaction--diffusion systems with chemotaxis. We show that chemotaxis can give rise to a striking nonmonotonic dependence of pattern formation on its strength, opening the possibility of re-entrant transitions between patterned and homogeneous states controlled by chemotaxis. In certain regimes, chemotaxis also induces additional heretofore unexplored instabilities. Furthermore, varying the strength of chemotaxis can drive morphological transitions between spot and stripe patterns.
summary: This paper analyzes pattern formation in reaction-diffusion systems coupled with chemotaxis. The authors demonstrate that the strength of chemotaxis can lead to nonmonotonic behavior, causing re-entrant transitions between patterned and uniform states. They use linear stability analysis and numerical simulations to map out these complex control regimes and morphological transitions.
main_problem: The study investigates how pattern formation in two-species reaction-diffusion systems is controlled by the strength of chemotaxis, specifically looking for nonmonotonic dependencies.
main_result: Chemotaxis can induce a striking nonmonotonic and re-entrant dependence of pattern formation on its strength, and it can also drive morphological transitions between spot and stripe patterns.
method: The analysis employs linear stability analysis (LSA) around uniform states to determine the selected wavevector ($k_c$), supplemented by direct numerical simulations (DNS) using pseudo-spectral methods.
model_or_system: The model is a generic two-species reaction-diffusion system incorporating mutual chemotaxis, exemplified by the chemotactic extension of the Selkov model for glycolysis in two dimensions.
key_observables: Pattern selection wavevector ($k_c$), pattern amplitudes ($\Delta\phi, \Delta\psi$), and the dependence of these on chemotaxis couplings ($\xi_1, \xi_2$).
important_parameters: Chemotaxis couplings ($\xi_1, \xi_2$), the strength of chemotaxis ($\xi$), and the system size ($L$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on linear stability theory and approximations for determining $k_c$; DNS studies are performed for specific parameter sets.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the nonmonotonic dependence of $k_c$ on $\xi$ for different chemotaxis regimes (reciprocal vs. nonreciprocal), and show corresponding variations in pattern amplitudes ($\Sigma\phi, \Sigma\psi$) across various $\xi$ values.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by setting up the reaction-diffusion system, performing LSA to find $k_c$'s dependence on chemotaxis strength, and then confirming these theoretical predictions and observing pattern transitions (spot/stripe) via DNS.
why_interesting: While focused on classical pattern formation, the concept of nonmonotonic control and re-entrant transitions driven by an external coupling (chemotaxis) is relevant to understanding phase transitions in complex quantum or open quantum systems.
